main.title: The Last Guy
main.subtitle: Lead the frightened crowd to the escape zone
main.summary: The Last Guy is Japan Studio's PlayStation 3 rescue game, released on 28 August 2008. Viewed from high above monster-infested cities, the player gathers stranded civilians into a following line and guides them towards safety before time expires. The leader is small against the city, making the route more important than a heroic close-up. Every rescued person adds to the group that must be brought through the streets. A useful shortcut for one character may be less safe once a long crowd is trailing behind, turning rescue into a problem of shape and movement.

cards.heading: Lead the frightened crowd to the escape zone
cards.text: The Last Guy is Japan Studio's PlayStation 3 rescue game, released on 28 August 2008. Viewed from high above monster-infested cities, the player gathers stranded civilians into a following line and guides them towards safety before time expires. The leader is small against the city, making the route more important than a heroic close-up. Every rescued person adds to the group that must be brought through the streets. A useful shortcut for one character may be less safe once a long crowd is trailing behind, turning rescue into a problem of shape and movement.

cards.heading: Find the people before choosing the route
cards.text: Thermal imaging helps locate survivors, while dashing and controlling the line provide tools for moving them around threats. The player has to judge when to gather a larger crowd and when to deliver those already following. A monster can make a familiar street dangerous, so the route must remain open to revision. Special VIPs offer extra rewards and can unlock further stages, encouraging attention beyond the most obvious groups. The task is readable from a distance: identify a stranded population, form a manageable line and bring it to the place where the city can finally be left behind.

cards.heading: A small figure gives real cities another scale
cards.text: The playable locations draw on cities across North America, Europe and Asia, using the overhead view to make buildings and streets part of a maze. Leaderboards and rescue totals give completed stages another reason to be revisited. The digital release followed a Japan-only preview and later received trophy support and additional downloadable material. Its distinctive effect comes from the distance of the camera. Individual figures are tiny, but the line accumulating behind the player makes the scale of a successful rescue visible, turning a growing crowd into both the reward and the responsibility carried through the level.

main.title: Infinite Undiscovery
main.subtitle: Cut the chains holding the moon
main.summary: Infinite Undiscovery is tri-Ace and Microsoft Game Studios Japan's Xbox 360 action role-playing game, first released in North America on 2 September 2008. Capell joins the Liberation Force in a journey to sever the chains that bind the moon, becoming part of a struggle larger than the life he previously knew. The party moves through the world and fights in real time, keeping decisions close to the action. Situations can continue developing even while a menu is open, giving preparation and immediate awareness a different relationship from a role-playing game that pauses whenever an item is selected.

cards.heading: Cut the chains holding the moon
cards.text: Infinite Undiscovery is tri-Ace and Microsoft Game Studios Japan's Xbox 360 action role-playing game, first released in North America on 2 September 2008. Capell joins the Liberation Force in a journey to sever the chains that bind the moon, becoming part of a struggle larger than the life he previously knew. The party moves through the world and fights in real time, keeping decisions close to the action. Situations can continue developing even while a menu is open, giving preparation and immediate awareness a different relationship from a role-playing game that pauses whenever an item is selected.

cards.heading: Borrow another companion's abilities
cards.text: The player controls Capell while other party members act alongside him. Connect actions allow access to a companion's skills, making the group useful beyond the abilities of the single character directly controlled. Some encounters involve several teams drawn from the larger cast, widening the scale of the situation. The player has to recognise which companion can answer a particular need while the battle continues around them. The system makes cooperation an active part of control: another character is not merely present, but provides something Capell can deliberately bring into the encounter.

cards.heading: A Japanese role-playing project for Xbox 360
cards.text: Square Enix published the game during a period when Microsoft was supporting several Japanese role-playing releases for its console. Hajime Kojima produced it, with Motoi Sakuraba composing the score and writers including Ryo Mizuno and Shoji Gatoh contributing to the story. International releases arrived within days of one another in September 2008. Reviews ranged from mixed to positive. The game's distinctive interest is the attempt to make a party adventure feel continuously active, allowing changing circumstances and other characters' abilities to remain present while the player decides what to do next.

main.title: Viva Piñata: Trouble in Paradise
main.subtitle: Make a garden worth visiting
main.summary: Viva Piñata: Trouble in Paradise is Rare's Xbox 360 gardening simulation, released in North America on 2 September 2008. The player reshapes a patch of land to attract brightly coloured piñata creatures, learning what each species needs before it will settle there. Plants, ponds and other residents turn the garden into a network of requirements. The sequel expands the original's collection and adds cooperative play, allowing another gardener to help with the same space. Its gentle appearance hides a game about observation, planning and managing the consequences of each new arrival.

cards.heading: Make a garden worth visiting
cards.text: Viva Piñata: Trouble in Paradise is Rare's Xbox 360 gardening simulation, released in North America on 2 September 2008. The player reshapes a patch of land to attract brightly coloured piñata creatures, learning what each species needs before it will settle there. Plants, ponds and other residents turn the garden into a network of requirements. The sequel expands the original's collection and adds cooperative play, allowing another gardener to help with the same space. Its gentle appearance hides a game about observation, planning and managing the consequences of each new arrival.

cards.heading: A visitor changes the whole garden
cards.text: A creature may need a particular plant, terrain or food source before becoming a resident. Meeting that condition can attract something else, so one improvement often begins another chain of decisions. The Piñarctic and Dessert Desert provide separate areas where creatures can be trapped and brought home. Sand and ice can later be introduced to the main garden to support them. An encyclopedia records preferences, giving the player a practical way to turn curiosity into a plan. The garden grows through these relationships rather than through decoration alone.

cards.heading: Share the work and the discoveries
cards.text: Two players can garden locally, with larger cooperative groups originally supported through Xbox Live. A Just for Fun mode removes several restrictions and threats, offering an easier space for experimentation. The Xbox Live Vision camera can read special cards to introduce creatures or items, connecting a physical collectible to the garden. Grant Kirkhope composed the music. Trouble in Paradise later joined Rare Replay on Xbox One, carrying its expanded version of the original idea to another console. Its pleasures remain the small discoveries that follow a carefully made change.

main.title: Spore
main.summary: Spore is a 2008 god game developed by Maxis and published by Electronic Arts for Windows and Mac OS X.

cards.heading: From a cell to a spacefaring species
cards.text: Spore is a 2008 god game developed by Maxis and published by Electronic Arts for Windows and Mac OS X. Designed by Will Wright, it covers many genres including action, real-time strategy, and role-playing games. Spore allows a player to control the development of a species from its beginnings as a microscopic organism, through development as an intelligent and social creature, to interstellar exploration as a spacefaring culture. It has drawn wide attention for its massive scope, and its use of open-ended gameplay and procedural generation. Throughout each stage, players are able to use various creators to produce content for their games. These are then automatically uploaded to the online Sporepedia and are accessible by other players for download.

cards.heading: Creation tools and reception
cards.text: Reviewers welcomed the tools for creating creatures, vehicles and buildings, but many found the individual stages shallow. The game also attracted controversy over SecuROM and its digital rights management restrictions. Spore's broad ambition and approachable creation tools remained central to the discussion around its release.

main.title: Pokémon Platinum
main.summary: Pokémon Platinum Version is a 2008 role-playing video game developed by Game Freak and published by The Pokémon Company and Nintendo for the Nintendo DS.

cards.text: Pokémon Platinum Version is a 2008 role-playing video game developed by Game Freak and published by The Pokémon Company and Nintendo for the Nintendo DS. The game is an enhanced version of the 2006 titles Pokémon Diamond and Pearl and is part of the fourth generation of the Pokémon video game series. It was released in Japan in September 2008 and internationally throughout 2009.

In Pokémon Platinum, players control either Lucas or Dawn and begin with one of three Pokémon provided by Professor Rowan. The mascot Pokémon is Giratina, which plays a central role in the story. While Giratina had only one form in Diamond and Pearl, it gains a new "Origin Form" in Platinum, introduced alongside the Distortion World, a new area featuring altered physics compared with the Sinnoh region where the game takes place. Gameplay follows traditional Pokémon mechanics: players explore towns, caves, and outdoor environments, capture and train Pokémon, and engage in turn-based battles.

Pokémon Platinum received generally positive reviews, holding aggregate scores of 84 on Metacritic and 83.14% on GameRankings. Critics praised it as one of the stronger entries in the series and noted the additions and refinements made over Diamond and Pearl, while some criticized it for being too similar to those games. Publications such as IGN, Nintendo Power, and GamePro highlighted its improvements; IGN ranked it ninth on its list of the best Nintendo DS games and nominated it as one of the best DS role-playing games of 2009. It was the fastest-selling video game in Japan at the time of its release and had sold 7.06 million copies worldwide by March 31, 2010.

main.title: Rock Band 2
main.subtitle: The shared tour becomes a platform for a growing music library
main.summary: Rock Band 2 developed the original band format with an online World Tour, drum training and a new disc selection built from master recordings.

cards.heading: Taking the band further
cards.text: Rock Band 2 first appeared on Xbox 360 in North America on September 14, 2008, with PlayStation 3, PlayStation 2 and Wii versions following later. Harmonix retained guitar, bass, drums and vocals for up to four players. Its 84-song disc selection uses master recordings rather than newly commissioned cover performances. Compatible downloadable music and an authorised export of much of the first game’s disc helped make the sequel feel like an expanding library, not an isolated setlist.

cards.heading: Practising and playing together
cards.text: World Tour extended the band’s journey into online play, while challenges offered other routes through the repertoire. Drum Trainer separated rhythmic patterns and fills from the pressure of a complete song, making the drum controller a place to practise as well as perform. A No Fail option made mixed-skill gatherings more welcoming. The refinements concentrate on continuity: keep the group playing, accommodate different abilities and let a familiar collection of songs acquire new uses.

main.title: Star Wars: The Force Unleashed
main.summary: Star Wars: The Force Unleashed is a 2008 action-adventure game developed and published by LucasArts, and part of The Force Unleashed  multimedia project.

cards.heading: Vader's secret apprentice
cards.text: LucasArts released Star Wars: The Force Unleashed in September 2008 across several home consoles and handheld systems. Its action follows Darth Vader's secret apprentice between the prequel and original film trilogies. The PlayStation 3 and Xbox 360 editions later received downloadable content, collected with additional material in the Ultimate Sith Edition.

cards.heading: Starkiller and the Rebel Alliance
cards.text: The project bridges the first two Star Wars trilogies, acting as an origin story for both the united Rebel Alliance and the Galactic Civil War depicted in the original trilogy. The game introduces a new protagonist named "Starkiller", a powerful Force user trained as Darth Vader's secret apprentice, who is tasked with hunting down Jedi survivors of the Great Jedi Purge while trying to keep his existence a secret. However, after he is tasked with planting the seeds of what would become the Rebel Alliance, which Vader plans to take advantage of to overthrow the Emperor, Starkiller begins to question his morality and to redeem himself slowly. Following The Walt Disney Company's acquisition of Lucasfilm in 2012, the game became part of the non-canonical Star Wars Legends continuity in 2014, and an alternative origin for the Rebel Alliance and the Galactic Civil War was given in other forms of Star Wars media, such as Star Wars Rebels and Andor.

cards.heading: Reception and a sequel
cards.text: Star Wars: The Force Unleashed received mixed reviews from critics, praising its story, voice acting, physics, art, and soundtrack, but criticizing its linear gameplay and technical issues. The game was a bestseller in the United States and Australia, with over 1,000,000 copies sold in its debut month. As of February 2010, the game had sold over 7,000,000 copies, and was the fastest-selling Star Wars video game of its time.  A sequel, Star Wars: The Force Unleashed II, was released in October 2010.

main.title: Kirby Super Star Ultra
main.summary: A collection of Kirby adventures returns on DS with new challenges, Helpers to share the action and touch-screen games built around quick reactions.

cards.heading: The game
cards.text: Kirby Super Star Ultra is HAL Laboratory's 2008 Nintendo DS platform-game collection. It remakes the 1996 Super NES game Kirby Super Star, known in Europe as Kirby's Fun Pak, with updated graphics, rendered story scenes and additional modes. Its adventures share Kirby's movement and copied powers while giving the player different goals.

cards.heading: Several reasons to start an adventure
cards.text: Spring Breeze provides a short journey through familiar Kirby action, but the next adventure can ask for something quite different. The Great Cave Offensive hides sixty treasures throughout its passages, encouraging careful searches and returns to missed rooms. Gourmet Race makes speed and food collection compete for attention as Kirby races King Dedede. Those changing objectives give the same basic movement another purpose: an enemy or a side route that slows a race may be exactly what matters during a treasure hunt.

cards.heading: Turn a power into a partner
cards.text: A copied power can also become a Helper. Kirby gives up the ability he is carrying to create a companion who fights alongside him, controlled by the game or by a second player through local wireless play. The choice changes the way the pair handles a room: an ability kept for Kirby gives him its attacks directly, while a Helper provides another body and another position from which to fight. Different enemy forms supply different partners, making familiar Copy Abilities useful in another way.

cards.heading: Another set of rules
cards.text: Ultra adds new challenges around that collection, including adventures for Meta Knight and a mode that lets the Helpers take on their own battles. The DS also contributes three touch-screen minigames. Kirby on the Draw tests how quickly a player can identify and hit a target; Kirby Card Swipe asks for a matching card before a rival reaches it. Up to four players can compete in the minigames locally, giving the cartridge a short, competitive interruption between its longer cooperative adventures.

main.title: Disaster: Day of Crisis
main.subtitle: One rescuer faces a very bad day
main.summary: Disaster: Day of Crisis is Monolith Soft's Wii action adventure following former rescue worker Raymond Bryce through a succession of natural catastrophes and terrorist attacks. Cinematic exploration, driving and shooting sequences place different immediate dangers in his path. Saving civilians gives the spectacle a practical focus beyond simply surviving the next collapse. The Wii Remote and Nunchuk perform actions suited to the current emergency, while the story continually changes the situation around Ray. Its structure resembles an escalating disaster film in which the player must keep finding the next workable response.

cards.text: Disaster: Day of Crisis is Monolith Soft's Wii action adventure following former rescue worker Raymond Bryce through a succession of natural catastrophes and terrorist attacks. Cinematic exploration, driving and shooting sequences place different immediate dangers in his path. Saving civilians gives the spectacle a practical focus beyond simply surviving the next collapse. The Wii Remote and Nunchuk perform actions suited to the current emergency, while the story continually changes the situation around Ray. Its structure resembles an escalating disaster film in which the player must keep finding the next workable response.

cards.heading: Survival includes taking a breath
cards.text: Ray's condition depends on more than the damage received in a fight. Strenuous activity drains stamina, while smoke and poisonous fumes affect his lungs. Food and opportunities to breathe fresh air help him recover. Rescuing another person can require moving obstacles, carrying someone to safety or completing a first-aid action before time runs out. These demands connect the large-scale catastrophes with the physical work of a rescuer. Reaching a safe position matters because it provides a chance to restore the condition needed for the next dangerous passage.

cards.heading: A different control for the next emergency
cards.text: Shooting sections use the Remote's pointer to aim, with cover and a zoom mode offering different ways to handle incoming fire. Driving instead uses the controller held sideways and tilted to steer. Other emergencies call for timed inputs or gestures with the Remote and Nunchuk. Rescuing civilians earns Survival Points that improve Ray's abilities, while combat rewards support weapon upgrades. The changing controls give each sequence an immediately recognisable task, moving between the responsibilities of keeping Ray alive, stopping an attacker and helping somebody else escape.

main.title: Wipeout HD
main.summary: Wipeout HD is a 2008 racing video game developed by Studio Liverpool and published by Sony Computer Entertainment for the PlayStation 3.

cards.text: Wipeout HD is a 2008 racing video game developed by Studio Liverpool and published by Sony Computer Entertainment for the PlayStation 3. It is the eighth instalment of the Wipeout series and the first on this platform. It was originally released digitally on the PlayStation Network in September 2008, before a major expansion pack titled Wipeout HD Fury came in July 2009, followed by a retail version made available in Europe in October that year.

The game revolves around players competing in the FX350 anti-gravity racing league, and features selected tracks from its predecessing PlayStation Portable games Wipeout Pure and Wipeout Pulse, although the content has been upgraded to render 1080p visuals in 60 frames per second, and supports stereoscopic 3D. Wipeout HD was developed by Studio Liverpool, who had desired to release a game for the PlayStation Store to stress that downloadable content was not reserved for smaller games. The game was delayed for a few months due to reports of it failing epilepsy tests.

Wipeout HD and its expansion pack received positive reviews upon release. Critics unanimously praised the game's 1080p visuals, smooth frame rate, and techno soundtrack – a feature many critics recognised as a hallmark of the Wipeout series. The game received controversy over its in-game advertising at the time of the Fury expansion pack's release, with many players complaining of extended loading times due to in-game advertisements. Wipeout HD, along with its Fury expansion pack, was also chosen as a free offering as part of Sony's "Welcome Back" programme due to the 2011 PlayStation Network outage. The expanded Fury version and the subsequent Wipeout 2048 were remastered for PlayStation 4 and released as Wipeout Omega Collection in 2017.
